title: Gaps and islands
summary: Ordered rows form islands (runs of consecutive rows) separated by gaps. lead finds the gaps; for islands, subtract row_number from a fixed-step sequence, or flag each row that starts an island and number the islands with a running sum. Then GROUP BY the island number.

examples.title: Missing days with lead, streaks with day - row_number

annotations.note: lead(day) puts the next existing day on each row. The last day has no next one, so next_day is NULL there, NULL > 1 is not true, and the WHERE drops the row.
date + int, date - int and date - date are day arithmetic. From 11-03 to 11-06 the hole is 11-04 to 11-05, two days.

Inside a streak, day and rn both grow by 1, so day - rn stays the same; a gap of k days shifts it by k. The value (2026-10-31) means nothing, only its sameness does. row_number returns bigint and there is no date - bigint operator, hence ::int.
Grouping on that constant turns each island into one row with its first day, last day and length. The same trick works on integer sequences such as invoice numbers (n - row_number).

examples.title: Status streaks per test: flag the changes, number them with a running sum

annotations.note: Çıkış didn't run in builds 102 and 104. The islands are consecutive runs of a test, not consecutive build numbers, so subtracting row_number from build would split them. This needs the general technique.

Step 1: a run starts an island when its status differs from the previous run's. On each test's first run lag is NULL, and IS DISTINCT FROM counts NULL versus 'passed' as different, so island 1 starts there.

Step 2: a running sum of the flags. Each 1 opens a new island number and the 0s keep the current one. The default RANGE frame is safe because build is unique within a test; with ties, peers would share a sum.
A view names the steps and lets two queries share them; the sandbox rolls it back with everything else. A CTE does the same inside one statement.

Step 3 is a plain GROUP BY on (test_case, island). current compares each island with the test's highest island number, a window over the grouped rows. Çıkış has failed three runs in a row, builds 103 to 106: the alert you want.
SQLSTATE 42P20: window function calls cannot be nested. The flag has to be computed one query level down before sum can run over it, which is the whole reason the technique has two levels.

examples.title: Sessions: islands separated by 30 minutes of inactivity

annotations.note: The ::time values below are local times; pinning the time zone keeps them the same on every server.

The break condition is a time gap: more than 30 minutes since the user's previous event opens a new session. On the first event lag is NULL, the comparison is NULL, and CASE falls through to ELSE 1. A NULL that happens to do the right thing deserves a comment in real code.
The same running sum as in example 2, ordered by (at, id) so that two events in the same instant can't become peers and share a number.

ayşe's first session lasts 70 minutes although the timeout is 30: each event only has to be within 30 minutes of the previous one, so sessions chain. emre's events are 31 minutes apart: two sessions of length zero.

use_cases: Missing data: days without a backup or upload, holes in invoice or ticket numbering
Streaks: consecutive failures of a test (alert at three in a row), consecutive days with activity
State history as intervals: 'passed builds 101 to 102, failed 103 to 104' from a per-run status log
Sessionization: splitting clickstreams or API calls into sessions by an inactivity timeout
Availability reports: outage periods from per-minute health checks
strengths: A few sorts and one pass each; the self-join and correlated-subquery versions compare every row with many others
Flag-and-sum works for any break condition: a changed value, a time gap, a threshold crossed, combined with PARTITION BY
The result is ordinary rows (from, to, length), ready for joins, filters or another GROUP BY, instead of a stream the application must fold
The work stays in the database, so an alert query returns two rows, not the full event history
weaknesses: Two or three nested query levels are hard to read without named steps (CTEs or views) and comments
Window functions can't be nested or filtered in place, which is what forces the extra levels
The row_number subtraction only works on a fixed-step sequence (consecutive integers or days); anything irregular needs flag-and-sum
Every partition is sorted; on a large event table the sort dominates unless an index supplies the order

pitfalls.title: <> instead of IS DISTINCT FROM in the flag
pitfalls.detail: If the compared value can be NULL (a skipped run), <> yields NULL, the CASE reads it as 'no change', and the NULL rows silently join the previous island.
pitfalls.bad: CASE WHEN status <> lag(status) OVER w THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
pitfalls.good: CASE WHEN status IS DISTINCT FROM lag(status) OVER w THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

pitfalls.title: lag inside sum() OVER
pitfalls.detail: Window function calls cannot be nested (SQLSTATE 42P20). Compute the flag in a subquery or CTE, then sum it one level up.
pitfalls.bad: sum(CASE WHEN status <> lag(status) OVER w THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER w
pitfalls.good: SELECT ..., sum(starts) OVER w FROM (SELECT ..., CASE WHEN ... lag(status) OVER w ... END AS starts FROM test_runs) AS flagged

pitfalls.title: Subtracting row_number when values repeat
pitfalls.detail: Two uploads on one day give that day two row numbers, so day - row_number changes in the middle of a streak and splits it. dense_rank numbers distinct values and keeps the key constant.

pitfalls.title: A running sum over a non-unique order
pitfalls.detail: With the default RANGE frame, rows that tie on the ORDER BY get the same sum, so an island that starts on a tied row can merge with the previous one. Add a unique column to the order.
pitfalls.bad: sum(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY at)
pitfalls.good: sum(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY at, id)

quiz.q: Days 1, 2, 3, 6, 7. What does `day - row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)` give?
quiz.why: Row numbers are 1 to 5: 1-1, 2-2, 3-3, 6-4, 7-5. The two days missing between 3 and 6 shift the key by 2.

quiz.q: Why does `sum(CASE WHEN status <> lag(status) OVER w THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER w` fail?
options: sum can't be used as a window function
Window function calls can't be nested; compute the flag in a subquery first
CASE isn't allowed in a window function's argument
quiz.why: PostgreSQL rejects a window call inside another window call's argument (SQLSTATE 42P20).

quiz.q: Events at 09:00, 09:20, 09:45 and 10:10, with a 30-minute inactivity timeout. How many sessions?
quiz.why: Each event is within 30 minutes of the previous one, so no break condition fires; sessions chain.

quiz.q: status can be NULL for a skipped run. Which flag starts a new island when NULL follows 'failed'?
quiz.why: Comparisons with NULL yield NULL, which CASE treats as false; IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a comparable value and returns true.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Window Functions (lag, lead, row_number, dense_rank)
PostgreSQL docs: Comparison Functions and Operators (IS DISTINCT FROM)
PostgreSQL docs: Date/Time Functions and Operators (date arithmetic)

body:
## Concept

"Gaps and islands" names a family of questions about ordered data: where does a sequence
have holes (**gaps**), and which runs of consecutive rows belong together (**islands**)?
The days a nightly upload didn't arrive, how many builds in a row a test has failed,
which clicks make up one session.

A table has no order, so "consecutive" is built from window functions, in two steps:
**mark** each row (compare it with its neighbour, or compute a key that stays the same
along a run), then **group** on the mark to get one row per island. Three techniques
cover nearly every case:

- **Gaps with `lead`:** put the next value on each row; a jump bigger than the step is a
  gap, from `value + 1` to `next - 1`.
- **Subtract `row_number`:** for a fixed-step sequence (integers, days), `value -
  row_number()` is constant inside an island and changes at every gap.
- **Flag and running sum:** set a flag to 1 on each row where an island starts (the
  value changed, too much time passed), then `sum(flag) OVER (ORDER BY ...)` numbers
  the islands. It works for any break condition.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python:** `itertools.groupby` starts a new group every time the key changes, so it
  groups *consecutive* equal values: islands, in one line, because an iterator has an
  order. SQL needs a window `ORDER BY` to supply the order, and the running sum plays the
  part of groupby's "new group starts here".
- **pandas:** `(s != s.shift()).cumsum()` is flag-and-sum written out: `shift` is `lag`,
  `!=` is the flag, `cumsum` is the running sum. NaN compares unequal to everything, so
  the first row starts a group, the role `IS DISTINCT FROM` plays here.
- **C/C++, Java, Go:** the loop is `if (cur != prev) island++;`. SQL splits those two
  statements across two query levels because a window function can't take another
  window function as its argument.

## How it works

Why `value - row_number` works: inside an island both grow by exactly one per row, so
their difference doesn't move. A gap of `g` missing values makes the value jump by
`g + 1` while the row number still grows by 1, so the difference jumps by `g`. If a value
can appear twice, `row_number` would still grow on the duplicate; `dense_rank` doesn't.

Flag-and-sum, on Giriş from example 2:

```
build    101     102     103     104     105     106
status   passed  passed  failed  failed  passed  passed
starts   1       0       1       0       1       0
island   1       1       2       2       3       3
```

The running sum only grows, and only where an island starts, so every island gets its
own number. From there it is ordinary `GROUP BY test_case, island`.

## Design notes

Name the steps. A CTE or view per step (`flagged`, `numbered`, then the grouped result)
makes the pattern recognizable; three anonymous nested subqueries make it a puzzle.

Default to flag-and-sum. It handles partitions, NULLs (with `IS DISTINCT FROM`), time
thresholds and combined conditions. Keep the `row_number` subtraction for clean
fixed-step sequences, where it is shorter. To list every missing day rather than ranges,
generate the calendar with `generate_series` and anti-join the data to it.

If a dashboard asks for streaks on every page load over a long history, consider
recording the transitions when they happen: a row per status change turns every island
into a stored range, and the window query becomes a lookup. An index on the partition and
order columns (here the primary key, `(test_case, build)`) can supply the sort order.

files.examples/01_days.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.windows.gaps-islands): number the rows, subtract, and consecutive rows share a key.
CREATE TABLE uploads (
  day date PRIMARY KEY            -- days the CI agent uploaded its results
);
INSERT INTO uploads VALUES
  ('2026-11-01'), ('2026-11-02'), ('2026-11-03'),
  ('2026-11-06'), ('2026-11-07'),
  ('2026-11-10'), ('2026-11-11'), ('2026-11-12'), ('2026-11-13');

-- Gaps: look at the next day; a jump of more than one day is a hole.
SELECT day + 1 AS gap_from, next_day - 1 AS gap_to,
       next_day - day - 1 AS missing_days
FROM (SELECT day, lead(day) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS next_day FROM uploads) AS d
WHERE next_day - day > 1
ORDER BY gap_from;

-- Islands: day and row number both grow by 1 inside a streak, so their
-- difference stays constant until a gap shifts it.
SELECT day,
       row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day) AS rn,
       day - row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)::int AS island
FROM uploads
ORDER BY day;

-- Group on that constant: one row per streak.
SELECT min(day) AS first_day, max(day) AS last_day, count(*) AS days
FROM (
  SELECT day, day - row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)::int AS island
  FROM uploads
) AS s
GROUP BY island
ORDER BY first_day;
files.examples/02_status_streaks.sql:
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  test_case text NOT NULL,
  build     int  NOT NULL,           -- CI build number; not every build runs every test
  status    text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (test_case, build)
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  ('Giriş', 101, 'passed'), ('Giriş', 102, 'passed'), ('Giriş', 103, 'failed'),
  ('Giriş', 104, 'failed'), ('Giriş', 105, 'passed'), ('Giriş', 106, 'passed'),
  ('Çıkış', 101, 'passed'), ('Çıkış', 103, 'failed'), ('Çıkış', 105, 'failed'),
  ('Çıkış', 106, 'failed');

-- Step 1: flag each row that differs from the previous one (lag), and
-- step 2: a running sum of the flags numbers the islands.
CREATE VIEW numbered AS
SELECT test_case, build, status, starts,
       sum(starts) OVER (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY build) AS island
FROM (
  SELECT test_case, build, status,
         CASE WHEN status IS DISTINCT FROM
                   lag(status) OVER (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY build)
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS starts
  FROM test_runs
) AS flagged;

SELECT * FROM numbered ORDER BY test_case, build;

-- Step 3: one row per island, and the current streak of each test.
SELECT test_case, status, min(build) AS from_build, max(build) AS to_build,
       count(*) AS runs,
       island = max(island) OVER (PARTITION BY test_case) AS current
FROM numbered
GROUP BY test_case, island, status
ORDER BY test_case, from_build;

-- The tempting one-step version: lag inside sum() OVER.
SELECT test_case, build,
       sum(CASE WHEN status <> lag(status) OVER w THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER w
FROM test_runs
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY build);
files.examples/03_sessions.sql:
SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Istanbul';

CREATE TABLE ui_events (
  id      int         PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id text        NOT NULL,
  at      timestamptz NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO ui_events VALUES
  (1, 'ayşe',  '2026-11-13 09:00+03'), (2, 'ayşe',  '2026-11-13 09:20+03'),
  (3, 'ayşe',  '2026-11-13 09:45+03'), (4, 'ayşe',  '2026-11-13 10:10+03'),
  (5, 'ayşe',  '2026-11-13 14:00+03'), (6, 'ayşe',  '2026-11-13 14:05+03'),
  (7, 'emre',  '2026-11-13 09:00+03'), (8, 'emre',  '2026-11-13 09:31+03');

-- A session ends after 30 minutes of silence. Islands again, but the
-- break condition is a time gap instead of a changed value.
SELECT user_id, session_no,
       min(at)::time AS started, max(at)::time AS ended,
       max(at) - min(at) AS length, count(*) AS events
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, at,
         sum(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY at, id) AS session_no
  FROM (
    SELECT user_id, at, id,
           CASE WHEN at - lag(at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY at, id)
                     <= interval '30 minutes'
                THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_session
    FROM ui_events
  ) AS flagged
) AS sessions
GROUP BY user_id, session_no
ORDER BY user_id, session_no;
